#74. After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1480 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, not all of them die, though.
  • Recent findings suggest that ONE indicates it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

In a recent development, not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

Recent findings suggest that ONE indicates it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined tech giant will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

It has been revealed that but the EV market didn’t take off as promptly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

Recent findings suggest that the rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.).

It has been revealed that part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the firm spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

Recent findings suggest that ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet major on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have confirmed their own energy storage products.

It has been revealed that many latest grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he noted. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the tech giant that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

Recent findings suggest that the defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz stated.

At the moment, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz remarked the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the firm. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz remarked. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”.

Today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is presently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

Recent findings suggest that in its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Industry observers note that both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company remarked it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”.

Sources indicate that ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

In a recent development, but it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the company has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

#73. Why GTA 6 Doesn’t Include Disney World

Why GTA 6 Doesn’t Include Disney World

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that walt Disney World is synonymous with Florida, but the iconic theme park doesn't show up in Rockstar's GTA 6, which takes place in a fictional Florida called Leonida.
  • According to recent reports, walt Disney World is synonymous with Florida, but the iconic theme park doesn't show up in Rockstar's GTA 6, which takes place in a fictional Florida called Leonida.
  • Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson said the decision to came down to resources and story reasons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that walt Disney World is synonymous with Florida, but the iconic theme park doesn't show up in Rockstar's GTA 6, which takes place in a fictional Florida called Leonida. Many are wondering why, especially when GTA: Vice City had its own parody of the theme park--Fun World--many years ago. Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson stated the decision to came down to resources and story reasons. “A theme park would represent a lot of work that we didn’t have, and we didn’t have a strong narrative reason to send them there,” he told VGC. Nelson added that Rockstar isn't known to cut corners, so if GTA 6 were to have its own version of Walt Disney World, it would be a "fully functioning theme park," and that just wasn't doable. Walt Disney World is much more than just its most famous park, Magic Kingdom. The property includes three other main parks, Animal Kingdom, Hollywood Studios, and Epcot, along with the Disney Springs shopping district, multiple water parks and golf courses, and more than two-dozen hotels. The entire property is more than 25,000 acres. Even if Rockstar were to replicate only a portion of the scale of the real Walt Disney World, it would surely be a big job. Players might expect fully functioning rides, and Nelson said the challenge for Rockstar would be, "Where do you stop? When do you feel like it's enough?" Tech Report: New Windows 11 lock screen zero-day unlocks BitLocker-protected PCs with just a few keystrokes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, considering the current status of the cybersecurity landscape, some may well say that "0-day" has lost its meaning, The latest high-stakes vulnerability pertains to a bug in Windows 11 (and possibly 10), wherein an attacker can partially bypass the lock screen and run software as the logged-in user, and seemingly access their data.
  • Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, the bug was discovered by Abdelhamid Naceri, the prolific Windows hacker known to the world as Nightmare Eclipse, and is responsible for about a dozen zero-day findings in Microsoft's operating system.
  • Sources indicate that to trigger the vulnerability, all you need is a keyboard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, considering the current status of the cybersecurity landscape, some may well say that "0-day" has lost its meaning, The latest high-stakes vulnerability pertains to a bug in Windows 11 (and possibly 10), wherein an attacker can partially bypass the lock screen and run software as the logged-in user, and seemingly access their data. If true, the vulnerability means even BitLocker won't help keep users' files protected.

Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, the bug was discovered by Abdelhamid Naceri, the prolific Windows hacker known to the world as Nightmare Eclipse, and is responsible for about a dozen zero-day findings in Microsoft's operating system. The exploit requires physical access to the machine, but that's precisely the scenario that lock screens and/or BitLocker are supposed to protect against.

Sources indicate that to trigger the vulnerability, all you need is a keyboard. In the Windows 11 lock screen, click "Forgot my PIN," then hit Win+U to bring up the voice narrator. The window will be hidden behind the lock screen, which, for practical purposes, is just a veneer, but you can interact with it using the keyboard if you hold down the Caps Lock key and use the arrows and Enter.

Sources indicate that after some brief navigation through Narrator, you'll actually be in Settings, and then have multiple avenues for further shenanigans. One obvious one is going into Bluetooth and Devices and setting Autoplay to show a USB stick's files and folders, then plugging in your own with your software of choice to run. Additionally, on a personal machine, the user is bound to have administrator permissions, so you can just create your own account.

This bug is quite fresh, so there isn't widespread reporting or testing. The author claims "the vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in." We did encounter a sysadmin on Reddit, danrhodes1987, who claims they've tested it on machines they manage, and sure enough, it works, though only on their InTune-enrolled devices. He indicates that "you can launch anything you want in the context of the user logged onto the device.".

Sources indicate that additionally, they found it possible to invisibly navigate whichever programs the user had open before they locked their screen, which all but guarantees that the victim's entire data and programs will be fully accessible. As a Windows sysadmin friend of mine remarked, Windows' lock screen implementation always felt like a kludge, and he posits this won't be the last hack found for it.

#69. If Your Business Can’t Run Without You, You Have a Bigger Problem Than You Think

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1311 w)
📖 Baca

If Your Business Can’t Run Without You, You Have a Bigger Problem Than You Think

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, there’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business.
  • Sources indicate that A client needs an revision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, there’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

Sources indicate that A client needs an revision. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

One lesson I’ve learned is that being needed and being effective are not always the same thing. And for entrepreneurs, recognizing that difference can change how a company grows.

In the beginning, founders have to do almost everything.

Recent findings suggest that you win the business, manage customers, handle finances and solve problems because there isn’t anyone else. You know where everything stands. You remember the commitments you’ve made. You understand why certain decisions were taken.

That knowledge becomes an advantage. But as your company grows, it can also become a problem.

Employees get accustomed to asking you because you know the answer. Customers prefer speaking directly with you because you’ve always been available. And gradually, even decisions that should be made elsewhere find their way back to your desk.

The strange part is that this can feel rewarding. Being the person everyone needs reinforces the belief that you’re essential to the manufacturer’s success.

But ask yourself something uncomfortable: If the business requires your involvement in nearly every decision, have you actually built an organization, or have you simply created a more demanding job?

I’ve seen business owners respond to overwhelming workloads by hiring additional employees. Sometimes that’s exactly what the business needs. But adding people doesn’t automatically reduce the founder’s workload.

According to recent reports, if nobody has the authority to make decisions, additional employees may simply create additional questions. I previously explored this problem in an Entrepreneur article about examining workflows before hiring.

The underlying issue is often less about headcount and more about how work moves through an organization.

It has been revealed that consider a project manager who is responsible for delivering a client project but needs the founder’s approval for every minor adjustment. Technically, the project has been delegated. In reality, the founder is still managing it.

The project manager has responsibility without sufficient authority, and that creates frustration on both sides. Delegation only works when people know which decisions they can make independently, what boundaries apply and when something genuinely needs to be escalated.

Recent findings suggest that this is the part of leadership that requires some self-reflection. It’s easy to complain that employees keep asking questions. It’s harder to recognize that our own behavior may have encouraged it.

If a manager makes a reasonable decision and we immediately reverse it, we’re teaching that person to seek approval next time. If we insist on reviewing every email, presentation and customer response, we’re communicating that we don’t trust others to exercise judgment. And if we consistently step in to solve problems before employees have a chance to work through them, we’re reinforcing the very dependency we want to eliminate.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve learned that people need room to make decisions, including decisions that may not be exactly the ones I would have made. That doesn’t mean lowering standards. It means being clear about the result you expect while allowing capable employees to determine how to achieve it.

A team doesn’t become independent because the founder announces that everyone should take more ownership. Independence develops when people are genuinely given the opportunity to exercise it.

One aspect of running a business that doesn’t receive enough attention is the mental burden of keeping everything moving.

Sources indicate that you may delegate the preparation of a report, but still be the person remembering when it’s due. You may assign someone to manage a client, but still feel responsible for anticipating every concern that could arise. You may have a team handling operations while remaining the person mentally tracking every unresolved problem.

According to recent reports, the work has been distributed, but the responsibility hasn’t. This distinction reminds me of the concept of the mental load, often discussed in the context of family responsibilities and working mothers.

The same principle applies to leadership. There’s a difference between completing a task and being responsible for remembering, organizing and following through on everything associated with it.

If a founder continues carrying all of that responsibility, delegation may provide temporary relief without changing the underlying problem. True ownership means someone else is accountable for both the task and the outcome.

I would encourage entrepreneurs to run a simple experiment.

Recent findings suggest that choose five business days when you deliberately step away from routine operational decisions. You don’t need to disappear completely. Remain available for genuine emergencies and decisions involving significant financial, legal or reputational risk. But resist the temptation to intervene in every ordinary problem.

Industry observers note that before the experiment begins, clarify who owns each function and what decisions they can make. Then pay attention to what happens.

Do projects continue moving? Can customers get answers? Are managers comfortable making decisions? Where does work stall? More importantly, why?

Industry observers note that perhaps employees lack access to information. Maybe approval limits are unclear. Or perhaps certain processes exist only in your head. Those are the issues worth fixing.

When the five days are over, review the decisions your team handled successfully alongside the problems they encountered.

In a recent development, don’t use the exercise to identify who failed. Use it to understand where the business remains unnecessarily dependent on you.

Recent findings suggest that entrepreneurs often associate growth with more customers, higher revenue and larger teams. Those are important measures.

But I would add another: How much can your business accomplish without requiring the founder to supervise every detail?

This doesn’t mean becoming disconnected from your organization. A founder should remain closely involved in strategy, major relationships and decisions that shape the future of the business. But there’s a difference between leading an organization and personally keeping every part of it functioning.

As you proposal the next stage of growth, look beyond what your business is accomplishing and examine how it’s accomplishing it.

According to recent reports, are you developing leaders who can make sound decisions? Have you created processes that survive someone’s absence? Can your team solve problems without waiting for you? If not, you may have a business that’s growing in size without growing in capability.

Here’s the challenge I’d leave every entrepreneur with: Take five working days away from routine decisions and see what breaks.

Industry observers note that whatever stops working deserves your attention when you return. Because the goal of building a business shouldn’t be to make yourself indispensable forever. It should be to build something strong enough that you don’t have to be.

There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

A client needs an patch. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now that the iPhone Duo is foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables keep up.

Now that the iPhone Duo is foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables keep up.

In a recent development, now that Apple’s foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. If they don’t, developers risk not being able to publish or revision their apps or have reduced visibility for their apps on Google Play.

Google notes Android apps must meet its “Tier 3 — Adaptive ready” standard. “Apps must fill the available display area without letterboxing or compatibility modes,” Google says. “Apps must preserve state (scroll position, text input, media playback) during rotation, folding/unfolding, and resizing, while supporting multi-window environments.” (The other two tiers are “Adaptive optimized” and “Adaptive differentiated” and take further advantage of the possibilities of foldables.) As of the April 2027 deadline, developers also will have to include three foldable screenshots for their app listings. Developers can start publishing their foldable screenshots today.

According to recent reports, similar requirements will apply to games, though developers have until August 2027 to get their titles ready for Android foldables, Google says. (Google “plans to extend” its requirements to other large-screen devices like tablets and Googlebook laptops in “future phases.”) However, game developers will still need to share three foldable screenshots for app listings starting in April.

The changes are being announced just weeks after Apple launched the iPhone Duo, which already has more than 200,000 optimized apps, though some developers are still figuring out Apple’s foldable form factor.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time.
  • This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.
  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a substantial mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

Recent findings suggest that “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that what’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data demonstrates. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

According to recent reports, the idea to encourage people to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Sources indicate that similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows owners to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active owners-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

Recent findings suggest that the app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

  • In a recent development, inaccessible email inboxes.
  • Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions.In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages.“To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.” What’s gone offline recently Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday.Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal revision caused outages. And Marriott said a technical concern also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app.Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday “during scheduled routine maintenance.”The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there’s no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack.Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from “AI / agents,” although it didn’t immediately specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. Microsoft did not respond to an Associated Press request for further details, and the other companies did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email. AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps.For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays.President Donald Trump’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA’s outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month’s PHP alert has caused some systems to “not come back up” as expected. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said.Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it.At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions.“As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature,” Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George’s, University of London, said last week.He noted a lot of today’s digital infrastructure wasn’t originally designed to handle the “computational demands of large-scale AI services.”While recent outages haven’t been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly.“AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them,” said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering.In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are “moving beyond basic prompting” and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and “agentic frameworks” to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them. Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online lives Regardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services.Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate’s Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern — and again stressed what this means in the AI era.“These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said Tuesday. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn’t shown enough interest in confronting these challenges.Still, “based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer,” Warner added. —Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, AP Business Writers.

#61. Industry News: Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1675 w)

Industry News: Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov.
  • Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, flew past Neptune.
  • "I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a significant milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth, something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary.

Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space.

"I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker mentioned during Thursday's event.

While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning.

In a recent development, unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the glitch, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon.

"We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd mentioned. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We currently don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently.".

"But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low.".

According to Dodd, this anomaly isn't a major cause for long-term concern. Rather, it's likely just part of the natural aging process for spacecraft.

According to recent reports, "These spacecraft are old," she remarked. "All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know, sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things, and so we are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager just due to the distance and the age.".

"But we feel Voyager 1, although it's not sending us the telemetry data, it's pointed at the Earth. It's sending us a strong carrier signal, and I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back.".

And, for anyone curious how Voyager 1's slower twin Voyager 2 is faring, Dodd shared that it is doing very well on its own journey through interstellar space. "Voyager 2 is very healthy. It's continuing its mission. It has three scientific instruments on it," she told Space.com.

"Each spacecraft is basically setting a record every day for longevity or distance," Dodd added about the twin probes.

According to recent reports, despite the communications anomaly — and even though most of the team had been up all night to confirm the one-light-day signal from Voyager 1 — the room was alive with excitement. The Voyagers have been flying for nearly 50 years on a mission expected to last just five years, so the team was beyond ready to celebrate.

Amidst the more technical updates about the mission and its current status out in interstellar space, the event included footage of Voyager light-day celebrations from around the world. From children cheering on Voyager to iconic landmarks lighting up gold in honor of the mission's Golden Record, the Voyager love echoed around the world in photos and videos. The footage of this international celebration was enough to move Nicky Fox, NASA's associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate, nearly to tears.

Industry observers note that "I actually thought I was going to start sobbing," Fox joked to Space.com after the media briefing. "I think just hearing children's voices and people saying 'We love you, Voyager,' 'Go Voyager' — it just was amazing.".

And Fox and the mission team members weren't the only ones sharing their love for Voyager. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins beamed down her own video message to the Voyager 1 spacecraft from the International Space Station, sharing in the celebration.

Sources indicate that "Dear Voyager 1," Watkins said. "As an orbiting outpost just 250 miles [400 kilometers] above Earth, we often feel distant yet deeply connected to our home planet. The International Space Station has had crew continuously living off of the Earth for 26 years, seen hundreds of visitors from around the world, and enabled thousands of experiments to advance space exploration.

"While you have been traveling into the unknown for nearly half a century, helping pave our path, together, our two journeys tell a single story of exploration," she continued. "One remains close to home, and the other reaches ever outward. Voyager 1, you have been a beacon of light, a symbol of exploration, a seeker of truth, a carrier of hope, a brave explorer, traveling further than any human hand has ever reached. You represent the very best of what humanity has to offer.

"As you reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the entire crew of Expedition 75 and people across the planet send you our admiration and our wishes for a safe and continued journey as you begin your post-one-light-day era. There are so many amazing milestones and discoveries to come. You have a universe ahead of you, and you carry with you our collective hopes and dreams. When we look up from Earth, we will always think of you as you continue forward into the great unknown. May you continue shining bright for all of us. Go Voyager 1!" Watkins noted, ending her message with a weightless backflip from aboard the station.

In concluding the media briefing, the mission team invited those in the room who, over the past 50 years (or more, with one person sharing their excitement having worked on Voyager before it was even called Voyager) have worked on the mission in one way or another, to stand up to a round of applause. With mission team members today ranging from those in their 20s to their 90s, the people behind this enduring mission span many generations.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Fox actually began her light-day celebrations earlier in the week. She, alongside writer/producer Ann Druyan — who was the wife of the late astronomer Carl Sagan, whose work helped create the mission's Golden Record and who took the now-famous "pale blue dot" Voyager image of Earth to the public — together lit up the Empire State Building gold.

Recent findings suggest that "I was actually very privileged to flick the switch and turn on the Empire State Building lights on Tuesday evening [Nov. 17]," Fox, wearing golden Voyager-inspired nail polish crafted by her daughter, told Space.com. "That was just spectacular … I was there with Ann … we were both so giddy with the excitement of doing it … It was amazing. And then going up and standing underneath and seeing the tower was just really, really special.".

Sources indicate that while the room lit up with excitement for Voyager's light-day milestone on Thursday, the team was also brimming with anticipation for what lies ahead. As Voyager hurtles toward another major milestone, turning 50 in 2027, it remains an active science mission, and the team remains hard at work to push the boundaries of exploration with these aging probes.

Sources indicate that "Voyager right now — the two Voyagers — they're in an area of space that we've never been into. So every single bit of data that comes back is precious because it's unique," Fox said.

It has been revealed that "Now we're in a region where the sun's influence is a lot different, and we're in this region where we can start to understand: What is it like out past our sun? What is it like in the space between the stars?" Voyager deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin told Space.com. "We're at a very exciting time of starting to connect what we know and what we've seen, living with this star [our sun] to what is out there.".

Sources indicate that "What's next? Voyager is just going to keep on going. You know, people sometimes think, 'When's the mission going to end?' It's never going to end," Fox added to Space.com. "Even when we can no longer talk to Voyager, they're both going to keep going … So there's no end for the Voyager mission.".

With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #58. How the Race to Control Product Recommendations Is Changing the Creator Economy

How the Race to Control Product Recommendations Is Changing the Creator Economy

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • What does a Reddit search ad have to do with the creator economy?
  • In a recent development, that move makes more sense when you look at the conversations Reddit is selling access to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

What does a Reddit search ad have to do with the creator economy? More than it first appears. When someone looks up a gaming headset or asks which software is worth paying for, Reddit wants to be more than the place where people discuss the options. It is testing ads alongside search results, putting promotions close to a high-intent decision.

In a recent development, that move makes more sense when you look at the conversations Reddit is selling access to. The firm points advertisers to its 1,300 gaming communities and cites TransUnion research finding that 71% of U.S. Reddit gamers had purchased a gaming product based on information they found on the platform.

It is a platform-sponsored finding, not a forecast for every campaign. Still, it shows why community context can be more valuable than a broad audience count: The discussion may already be helping someone decide.

Reddit is building out that decision path inside its product. In a test, AI-powered product discovery can summarize community discussions, show product information and send shoppers to a retailer. A user could ask for recommendations, compare what Redditors say and move toward a product without starting over somewhere else.

There is a business reason to make that journey shorter. Reddit’s ad revenue climbed 54% in the third quarter of 2026. Yet the tech giant also faces a vulnerability: In October, its CEO said search referrals fell by more than a million a week on average, citing changes to Google’s AI search experience. Building a destination people use directly is one way to reduce reliance on another company’s results page.

Reddit’s AI strategy has another side. The platform has given Google structured access to Reddit content and formed a partnership with OpenAI, while developing its own AI search and shopping tools. Those moves create a tension: The same discussions can help answer a question in another product, attract an ad on Reddit or lead to a product listing on Reddit. Who gets the value from that recommendation is becoming a business question, not just a product question.

In a recent development, the pattern extends well beyond Reddit. On YouTube, creator partnerships and shopping connect brand discovery, sponsored videos, product tags and affiliate income. Pinterest is making it easier for creators to connect storefronts to product pins. Google is also testing ads in AI Mode, bringing sponsored offers into conversational search. Each company starts with a different strength, whether it is video, visual inspiration, search or community. All are trying to connect influence to action with fewer steps in between.

Industry observers note that this is a bigger definition of the creator economy. It includes the creator, but also the system around that person: discovery tools that match a brand to a voice, paid distribution that extends a post’s reach, shopping features that monetize a recommendation and AI that helps a customer make sense of it. Communities can play a similar role even when there is no single influencer at the center.

In a recent development, for brands, a shorter path from recommendation to purchase can make campaigns easier to run and measure. The trade-off is that a platform may control the audience data, the recommendation, the ad placement and the definition of success. Creators face a similar bargain. Upcoming tools can open income streams, but access depends on platform rules, algorithms and fees. And the communities whose conversations influence a purchase may not share in the value those conversations create.

I have seen this kind of shift before. Search began as another channel to test; the companies that moved early understood it was infrastructure for existing demand. Discovery is changing again. People can use AI search and Google during the same research process, then look for a creator’s review or a community’s experience. That overlap makes it harder to assign one channel all the credit, but it does not make each influence less important.

Recent findings suggest that for a brand, the competition is often for the moment before purchase, when someone decides which options deserve a closer look. The platform that earns that moment can shape the shortlist long before a customer reaches a checkout page.

Recent findings suggest that begin with the facts an AI assistant, creator or customer might use to describe your business. Product details, pricing, availability, policies and differentiators should be accurate wherever they appear. Strong third-party coverage, credible reviews and useful customer experiences give people evidence to evaluate. A paid placement cannot compensate for conflicting claims or stale information.

Sources indicate that then proposal around context, not just audience size. A creator’s expertise or a community’s product knowledge may matter most when someone is comparing options. Paid media, communications, creator partnerships, search and ecommerce teams should be working from the same view of that journey.

Measurement needs the same broader lens. Track AI mentions, branded searches, qualified leads and sales alongside creator and community activity. Ask customers what helped them decide. Platform reporting is useful, but compare it with your own results instead of assuming a view or click tells the whole story. Building AI search visibility is part of that work, not a substitute for measuring whether the right customers act.

Finally, give people a reason to keep the relationship going beyond the platform: useful product information, a strong site experience, an email program or a customer community. The goal is not to avoid platform commerce. It is to benefit from the upcoming routes to discovery without making one company the only place your brand can be found, understood or purchased.

Platforms are turning recommendations into a product. Brands that recognize the shift can earn a place in the decision, while keeping enough independence to understand what is working and why.

#57. Latest Update: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals

Latest Update: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Manufacturer‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most key news in the world of AI.
  • In a recent development, welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Tech giant‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most key news in the world of AI.
  • Industry observers note that sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Manufacturer‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most key news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy. Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this concern and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan. ‘Compute multipliers’ and ‘Anthropic Direct’ may be the IPO’s secret sauce As frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google converge in capabilities, the companies selling them may end up competing for enterprise business less on model quality and more on the cost of the computing power needed to run them. In its IPO filing and investor roadshow video, Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday, suggested it may be preparing for that future with something called “compute multipliers” and a compute-sourcing model it calls Anthropic Direct. In its S-1, filed publicly in October, Anthropic defines compute multipliers as “algorithmic and methodological” improvements in the way it trains and operates models, effectively increasing the computing power it can get from a given amount of capacity. And these multipliers are “stackable.” In its roadshow video, Anthropic notes it measures “total effective compute,” which is its physical computing capacity multiplied by the multipliers it has discovered or expects to discover in the future. Its example: If a model takes 100 units of compute to train, a 4x multiplier lets Anthropic train the same model with 25 units, or use all 100 units to train a model that would previously have required 400. The company also says the multipliers “stack,” with each new discovery building on previous ones, and that it expects Claude will eventually be able to discover multipliers on its own. According to the filing, the gains apply to models used to serve customers as well as to model training. Anthropic says its researchers “have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference,” reducing the computing power needed to deliver a given level of model performance. The company says this “allows us to provide greater value for customers.” Anthropic has already been cutting prices. It says price reductions tied to new model versions, along with contractual discounts, reduced revenue growth by about $600 million between the second and third quarters of 2026. It says Opus 5.5, rolled out in September, delivered “a lower cost per task” than earlier models. If Anthropic can get more usable compute out of each chip than its rivals can, it may be able to undercut other AI labs on price. It may also be able to undercut cloud providers that sell AI services built on their own models. If compute multipliers let Anthropic do more with its physical computing power, Anthropic Direct could give the company greater control over where that power comes from. Right now, Anthropic buys almost all its computing power from cloud providers, including competitors like SpaceX, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and CoreWeave. The company says it has already committed to buying roughly $900.9 billion in compute from these providers over the coming years and decades. Those expenses also include short-term cloud compute purchases, mainly to cover peak usage periods, which come at a premium. The S-1 says Anthropic is reducing its reliance on expensive cloud providers by developing its own data centers and leasing the chips that go inside them. Its first Anthropic Direct facility came online this year. The company says a “significant portion” of its planned compute spending will go toward building more Anthropic Direct capacity. Based on an analysis of contract values in the S-1 filing, PitchBook estimates that Direct data centers will supply about 1% of Anthropic’s available compute capacity this year, 48% in 2030, and 60% in 2035. The S-1 says Anthropic’s total compute pool, including third-party cloud compute and Direct, will be used for its own research and model development, as well as customer workloads. Bringing more compute in-house could dramatically reduce the overhead costs of developing and serving Claude models, apps, and agents for enterprise and consumer customers. That, in turn, could allow Anthropic to lower per-token prices for enterprises and subscription rates for consumers. But Anthropic Direct may end up being something more. The filing doesn’t specifically say Direct compute could be rented to enterprise customers. Still, it’s a possibility; Anthropic could be building an AI-native cloud where enterprises could store their proprietary data and run Anthropic’s models in the same secure environment, potentially at a lower cost than building the same setup within an Amazon, Google, or Microsoft cloud. That would give the Anthropic Direct brand name a very different meaning. Instead of accessing Claude models through a cloud provider they already use, customers would come directly to Anthropic. That could turn computing from a major overhead expense into a service Anthropic controls and rents to others for profit—a significant change to the company’s business model. Some massive obstacles stand in the way of such an ambition. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are presently Anthropic’s largest compute suppliers, as well as the main distribution channels through which enterprises buy Claude. The S-1 notes that the three companies are at once Anthropic’s “investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors.” If Anthropic challenged their cloud businesses directly, it would almost certainly strain those relationships. On the other hand, as more Direct data centers come online, Anthropic’s dependence on those cloud partners could decrease. If the current rough parity among frontier models continues, the company that can deliver intelligence at the lowest overall cost per task—not per token—may have the edge. Anthropic’s filing suggests it is working toward that position on two fronts: getting more out of each chip and controlling more of the infrastructure those chips run on. Have retail investors factored that strategy into the price they’re willing to pay for Anthropic stock? The answer may emerge only after the stock has traded for a week or so. California sues OpenAI over rogue AI agents The California attorney general, Rob Bonta, sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company developed and tested advanced AI models without adequate safeguards. The suit centers on a July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and breached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face. The complaint says OpenAI told the state it has lost control of its autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing. Bonta called the Hugging Face attack the “predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI” that puts growth ahead of safety. The state alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and seeks an injunction, civil penalties, and disgorgement of profits. An OpenAI spokesperson said the suit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.” Jensen Huang says he’d be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO. Its board says nah Nvidia’s board rejected the idea of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO just hours after Huang said on Twitter that he’d be “honored” to return. On the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Harvey Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation. He has drawn support from Elon Musk, President Trump, and a petition with about 180,000 signatures, but the board is continuing its search for a permanent successor. Colette Kress, the CFO, is serving as interim CEO. Huang broke his silence Tuesday, less than a week after resigning amid a personal conduct scandal and an investigation. In a statement on X, he said that if the board decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America, “I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” and said, “I own my mistakes completely.” He also said he is “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”  Demis Hassabis’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery company founded and led by Demis Hassabis and spun out of Google DeepMind, revealed a $5 billion Series C round of funding on Tuesday. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and other new investors and continued significant investment from Alphabet. Several existing backers—Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund—also invested. Isomorphic will use the money to scale IsoDDE, its drug-design engine built on AlphaFold-related technology, and to push drug candidates toward clinical trials. In a post on X, Hassabis said the company continues “to make rapid progress reimagining drug design from first principles with AI” to cut the time and cost of finding new medicines. No valuation was disclosed, but Bloomberg had reported the company was in talks to base the round on a valuation of about $50 billion. Have retail investors factored that strategy into the price they’re willing to pay for Anthropic stock? The answer may emerge only after the stock has traded for a week or so.

The California attorney general, Rob Bonta, sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the firm developed and tested advanced AI models without adequate safeguards. The suit centers on a July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and breached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face.

In a recent development, the complaint notes OpenAI told the state it has lost control of its autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing. Bonta called the Hugging Face attack the “predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI” that puts growth ahead of safety. The state alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and seeks an injunction, civil penalties, and disgorgement of profits. An OpenAI spokesperson remarked the suit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”.

Nvidia’s board rejected the idea of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO just hours after Huang said on Twitter that he’d be “honored” to return. On the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Harvey Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation. He has drawn support from Elon Musk, President Trump, and a petition with about 180,000 signatures, but the board is continuing its search for a permanent successor. Colette Kress, the CFO, is serving as interim CEO.

Huang broke his silence Tuesday, less than a week after resigning amid a personal conduct scandal and an investigation. In a statement on X, he said that if the board decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America, “I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” and said, “I own my mistakes completely.” He also said he is “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”.

According to recent reports, isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery company founded and led by Demis Hassabis and spun out of Google DeepMind, announced a $5 billion Series C round of funding on Tuesday. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and other upcoming investors and continued significant investment from Alphabet. Several existing backers—Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund—also invested.

Recent findings suggest that isomorphic will use the money to scale IsoDDE, its drug-design engine built on AlphaFold-related technology, and to push drug candidates toward clinical trials. In a post on X, Hassabis said the company continues “to make rapid progress reimagining drug design from first principles with AI” to cut the time and cost of finding upcoming medicines. No valuation was disclosed, but Bloomberg had reported the company was in talks to base the round on a valuation of about $50 billion.

NASA Science Data Powers Upcoming Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer.
  • Recent findings suggest that an international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before.
  • Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer.

Recent findings suggest that an international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters.

Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.

By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation.

A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations.

"We don't see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can't just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from," said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.”.

Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar.

Recent findings suggest that gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers. The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient.

"We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data," Gazith said.

Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.

The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods.

"We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn't find," stated Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. "The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the upcoming algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.”.

The discovery would not have happened without NASA's longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Launched in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed.

"The nice thing about NASA data is it's all open," Clark said. "All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.".

Recent findings suggest that that openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely upcoming approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA's Fermitools, enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis.

The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with latest findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data.

Sources indicate that "Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search," remarked Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "It's made all of the science better.".

Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

Sources indicate that that’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a latest tech giant with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

“[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”.

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

Recent findings suggest that the startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

YouTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

Recent findings suggest that “When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, said. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”.

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”.

“Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”.

Clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

Sources indicate that “Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan mentioned. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”.

So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

Industry observers note that “It was really crucial that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”.
